## Principle

A heat exchanger transfers heat from a hot stream to a cold stream across a solid wall that keeps the streams apart. The hot stream emerges colder than it entered, and the cold stream emerges warmer, and the transfer can continue, in any part of the unit, only while a temperature difference exists between the streams there. The overall balance is closed by the streams themselves: the heat given up by the hot stream reappears as heat taken up by the cold stream, losses to the surroundings aside. On either side, the load is determined by the mass flow rate, the specific heat capacity, and the temperature change of that stream.

Heat leaving the hot stream crosses, in succession, the hot-side fluid film, the wall, and the cold-side fluid film, and fouling deposited on the surfaces adds a further layer to the path. These resistances act in series, and the overall coefficient gathers them into a single measure of how readily the unit, as built, passes heat. A clean unit of a given construction has its own coefficient, which declines as fouling builds up, a decline that forms part of the unit's behaviour in service.

Under the usual arrangement, the temperature difference is greatest where the entering hot stream first encounters the leaving cold stream, and least where the two streams part company. The average the sizing relation calls for is the log-mean temperature difference, constructed from the differences at the two ends. With the coefficient and the area, the log-mean completes the sizing relation: the load carried by the unit is the product of the three.

Countercurrent flow, in which the streams move against one another, maintains a serviceable temperature difference along the whole length, and even permits the cold stream to be heated beyond the hot stream's leaving temperature. Parallel flow, in which the streams enter together, spends its temperature difference early and can never bring the two outlet temperatures across one another. The narrowest gap between the streams, commonly termed the pinch, governs the economics of the choice, because the area rises steeply as the pinch narrows, the mean driving force falling whilst the load remains unchanged.

## Equipment

The shell-and-tube exchanger is the general-purpose form against which the others are usually judged. A bundle of tubes carries one stream, whilst a shell around the bundle carries the other stream across the tubes. Baffles hold the tubes in place and force the shell-side stream to cross the bundle repeatedly, rather than running along it, which keeps the shell-side coefficient up. Where the design calls for a higher velocity, the tube-side stream may make more than a single pass through the bundle. This form tolerates the highest pressures and temperatures of any common form, is understood by every fabricator, and opens for inspection; its tube side cleans readily whilst its shell side does not, which is why a dirty stream is put through the tubes whenever the choice is free.

The plate exchanger builds its surface from a pack of thin corrugated plates, gasketed around their edges, with the streams in alternate gaps. The corrugations promote turbulence even at low velocities, the coefficient is high, and the pack provides a great deal of area in a small volume. The pack unbolts for cleaning and for adding or removing plates. Its ceiling is firmly set by the gaskets, which bound the pressure and the temperature of the service.

The double-pipe exchanger, quite simply a pipe within a pipe, suits small duties, is easily extended, and is at home at high pressures. The air cooler employs air itself as the cold stream: fans drive air across finned tubes, the fins compensating for the poor film coefficient of a gas, and the form is chosen where cooling water is scarce or expensive. The selection among the forms turns on the duty, the pressures and temperatures, the fouling the streams bring, and the cleaning the service will demand over the unit's life.

## Worked example

This worked example rates an installed exchanger against a duty. The task, with its data, is as follows: a hot process stream is to be cooled by a cold utility stream between terminal temperatures the process has specified, and an existing unit of known area and construction is offered for the service. The question is whether the installed area can carry the load at the stated terminal temperatures.

The load is fixed first, by the balance on the hot stream, using its mass flow rate, its specific heat capacity, and the specified fall in temperature. The balance then predicts the cold stream's rise in temperature, which is checked for consistency against the terminal temperatures stated in the task; a task whose two sides disagree is corrected before any sizing is attempted, because no exchanger can satisfy a balance that does not close.

From the terminal temperatures follow the two end differences, paired for countercurrent flow: the entering hot stream against the leaving cold stream at one end, the leaving hot stream against the entering cold stream at the other. The log-mean temperature difference is computed as the difference of the two end differences divided by the natural logarithm of their ratio, and stands as the driving force of the rating. The coefficient is estimated for the installed construction and the fluids stated, with allowance for the fouling the service is expected to need. The required area is the load divided by the product of the coefficient and the log-mean difference.

The required area is set against the installed area. Where the installed area exceeds the requirement, the unit carries the duty, and the excess is the margin the rating reports. Where the installed area falls short, the unit cannot carry the duty at the stated terminal temperatures, and the shortfall, not any verdict on the unit, is the result, since the same unit may serve at a relaxed terminal temperature. The example closes with the pressure drop on each side, calculated for the installed unit and read against the process allowances, because an exchanger that passes on area but fails on pressure drop does not serve.

## Limits

The rating and sizing methods of this chapter share the assumptions of the simple model, and the model fails wherever those assumptions fail. A stream that condenses or boils inside the unit holds its temperature whilst its enthalpy changes, so the temperature profile along the unit is no longer the one from which the log-mean is built. The remedy is to divide the unit where the regime changes, and to treat each part on its own profile.

Properties that change strongly with temperature break a second assumption, the constant coefficient. The film resistances depend on viscosity and conductivity, and a unit whose streams change temperature widely has a coefficient that changes along its length. A single coefficient then averages what the design needed to follow, and the error falls on the area in proportion. Fouling breaks a third assumption, in service rather than on paper: the coefficient used in the calculation belongs to the surface the calculation imagines, whereas deposits move the real coefficient away from it from the first day of operation.

It says nothing about the pressure drop a design imposes, nothing about tube vibration under cross-flow, nothing about the expansion stresses between a hot bundle and a cooler shell, and nothing about the mechanical codes the vessel must meet. Each of those questions is answered by its own method, and a design is complete only when all are answered. What the simple model delivers is the area a duty requires, on a stated set of assumptions. Those assumptions are listed here so the delivery can be weighed: where they hold, the area is sound; where they fail, the area is the first figure to re-examine.
